key_insight: A soft robotic hand exoskeleton can restore intentional grasping in people with severe hand paralysis by adding the missing hand motions needed for dexterous control. The device helps users perform meaningful daily tasks, including feeding, with a lightweight wearable design.
problem_solved: Severe hand impairment often leaves people unable to open, position, or stabilize the hand for functional grasping. This paper addresses the lack of practical, wearable assistance that can recover more natural, dexterous hand use.
method: Designed a lightweight textile-based soft hand exoskeleton for wearable assistance.
Added wrist dorsiflexion support to improve hand positioning for grasping.
Integrated an active opposable thumb to increase hand articulations and enable more dexterous grasps.
impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this shows how intelligent assistive robotics can translate sensing, actuation, and human-centered design into real functional gains. It highlights the importance of embodied systems that restore intent-to-action in rehabilitation and human augmentation.
visual_elements: Before/after illustration of a paralyzed hand versus assisted grasping with the exoskeleton
Exploded view of the textile glove showing wrist dorsiflexion and active thumb components
Icon sequence of everyday tasks enabled, such as holding utensils and feeding
Simple comparison diagram showing increased hand articulation and grasp range
paper_title: A dexterous soft hand exoskeleton restores intentional grasping in individuals with severe hand impairment
paper_authors: John Nassour, Nicolas Berberich, Daniel Utpadel-Fischler, Tobias Wächter, Gordon Cheng
